claim: ADSL functions in de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) and the purine nucleotide cycle.
source: Adenylosuccinate lyase (ADSL) functions in de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) and the purine nucleotide cycle.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and is supported by the schematic in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing ADSL's role in both pathways.

claim: ADSL deficiency (ADSLD) causes numerous neurodevelopmental pathologies, including microcephaly and autism spectrum disorder.
source: ADSL deficiency (ADSLD) causes numerous neurodevelopmental pathologies, including microcephaly and autism spectrum disorder.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to clinical literature in the introduction.

claim: ADSLD patients have normal serum purine nucleotide levels.
source: ADSLD patients have normal serum purine nucleotide levels but exhibit accumulation of dephosphorylated ADSL substrates, S-Ado, and SAICAr
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and referenced to prior clinical observations in the introduction (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015; Stone et al., 1998).

claim: ADSLD patients exhibit accumulation of dephosphorylated ADSL substrates, S-Ado, and SAICAr.
source: ADSLD patients have normal serum purine nucleotide levels but exhibit accumulation of dephosphorylated ADSL substrates, S-Ado, and SAICAr
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to clinical literature (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015).

claim: SAICAr has been implicated in neurotoxic effects through unknown mechanisms.
source: the latter being implicated in neurotoxic effects through unknown mechanisms
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citation to Stone et al., 1998 in the introduction.

claim: Diminished AMP levels resulting from ADSL depletion result in increased DNA damage signaling and cell cycle delays.
source: Using specific interventions to compensate for reduced purine levels or modulate SAICAr accumulation, we found that diminished AMP levels resulted in increased DNA damage signaling and cell cycle delays
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 1 and 2 showing that nucleoside supplementation rescues DNA damage and cell cycle phenotypes.

claim: Primary ciliogenesis is impaired specifically by loss of ADSL or administration of SAICAr.
source: while primary ciliogenesis was impaired specifically by loss of ADSL or administration of SAICAr
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 5 showing ciliogenesis defects that are not rescued by nucleosides but are rescued by PAICS inhibition and phenocopied by SAICAr treatment.

claim: ADSL-deficient chicken embryos displayed impaired neurogenesis and microcephaly.
source: ADSL-deficient chicken and zebrafish embryos displayed impaired neurogenesis and microcephaly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing reduced SOX2+ and ELAVL3/4+ cells in chicken neural tubes.

claim: ADSL-deficient zebrafish embryos displayed impaired neurogenesis and microcephaly.
source: ADSL-deficient chicken and zebrafish embryos displayed impaired neurogenesis and microcephaly.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 8 showing pinhead phenotype and reduced neuronal cell numbers.

claim: Neuroprogenitor attrition in zebrafish embryos was rescued by pharmacological inhibition of DNPS, but not increased nucleotide concentration.
source: Neuroprogenitor attrition in zebrafish embryos was rescued by pharmacological inhibition of DNPS, but not increased nucleotide concentration.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing MTX treatment rescues Sox2+ and Elavl3/4+ cell numbers while nucleoside supplementation does not.

claim: Zebrafish embryos depleted of Adsl displayed phenotypes commonly linked to ciliopathies.
source: Zebrafish also displayed phenotypes commonly linked to ciliopathies.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in Figures 6 and 7 showing hydrocephalus, heart looping defects, laterality defects, and shorter cilia in the Kupffer's vesicle.

claim: Both reduced purine levels and impaired DNPS contribute to neurodevelopmental pathology in ADSLD.
source: Our results suggest that both reduced purine levels and impaired DNPS contribute to neurodevelopmental pathology in ADSLD
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the differential rescue of phenotypes by nucleoside supplementation versus PAICS/MTX inhibition throughout the manuscript.

claim: Defective ciliogenesis may influence the ADSLD phenotypic spectrum.
source: and that defective ciliogenesis may influence the ADSLD phenotypic spectrum.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by the observation of ciliopathy-related phenotypes in zebrafish and ciliogenesis defects in human cells.

claim: ADSL is a conserved homotetrameric enzyme.
source: Adenylosuccinate lyase (ADSL) is a conserved homotetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the eighth reaction in the de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) pathway and also participates in the purine nucleotide cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019.

claim: ADSL catalyzes the eighth reaction in the de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) pathway.
source: Adenylosuccinate lyase (ADSL) is a conserved homotetrameric enzyme that catalyzes the eighth reaction in the de novo purine synthesis (DNPS) pathway and also participates in the purine nucleotide cycle (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutations in ADSL cause adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency (ADSLD), an autosomal recessive disorder.
source: Mutations in ADSL cause adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency (ADSLD), an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by defects in purine metabolism and heterogeneous neurological phenotypes
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to clinical literature (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015).

claim: ADSLD is characterized by defects in purine metabolism and heterogeneous neurological phenotypes including lack of eye-to-eye contact, auto-aggressive behavior, speech impairment, mild psychomotor delay, transient contact defects, autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy, and in some cases, microcephaly, encephalopathy, ataxia, or coma vigil.
source: Mutations in ADSL cause adenylosuccinate lyase deficiency (ADSLD), an autosomal recessive disorder characterized by defects in purine metabolism and heterogeneous neurological phenotypes that include lack of eye-to-eye contact, auto-aggressive behavior, speech impairment, mild psychomotor delay, transient contact defects, autism spectrum disorder, epilepsy, and in some cases, microcephaly, encephalopathy, ataxia, or coma vigil (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to clinical literature (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015).

claim: Over 100 ADSLD patients have been diagnosed to date.
source: While the incidence of ADSLD has not been fully established, over 100 patients have been diagnosed to date and subcategorized based on their symptoms that range from premature death to milder developmental and behavioral disorders (Jurecka et al., 2015; http://www.adenylosuccinatelyasedeficiency.com/).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Jurecka et al., 2015 and a website.

claim: ADSLD can be diagnosed by detecting elevated levels of SAICAR, S-AMP, SAICAr, and S-Ado in bodily fluids.
source: ADSLD can be diagnosed by detecting elevated levels of the substrates of ADSL, SAICAR (also referred to as SZMP), and S-AMP, as well as their dephosphorylated riboside forms, SAICAr and S-Ado, in bodily fluids (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984.

claim: Normal levels of purine nucleotides were detected in serum from ADSLD patients.
source: As normal levels of purine nucleotides were detected in serum from ADSLD patients, the accumulation of S-Ado, and particularly SAICAr, was proposed to play a role in the disease pathology (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015; Stone et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to clinical literature (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015; Stone et al., 1998).

claim: The accumulation of S-Ado, and particularly SAICAr, was proposed to play a role in ADSLD disease pathology.
source: As normal levels of purine nucleotides were detected in serum from ADSLD patients, the accumulation of S-Ado, and particularly SAICAr, was proposed to play a role in the disease pathology (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015; Stone et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to clinical literature (Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984; Jurecka et al., 2015; Stone et al., 1998).

claim: In yeast, ADSL (Ade13) loss provokes genomic instability and is lethal.
source: In yeast, ADSL (Ade13) loss provokes genomic instability and is lethal (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019; Giaever et al., 2002; Pinson et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to yeast studies (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019; Giaever et al., 2002; Pinson et al., 2009; Chen et al., 2016).

claim: Lethality in yeast from ADSL loss can be rescued by deletion of DNPS enzymes upstream of ADSL or the transcription factors that regulate the pathway.
source: Lethality in yeast can be rescued by deletion of a number of DNPS enzymes upstream of ADSL, or the transcription factors that regulate the pathway, indicating that the accumulation of metabolic intermediates, rather than impaired DNPS, underlies the toxicity (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to yeast studies (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019; Chen et al., 2016).

claim: In yeast, the accumulation of metabolic intermediates, rather than impaired DNPS, underlies the toxicity of ADSL loss.
source: Lethality in yeast can be rescued by deletion of a number of DNPS enzymes upstream of ADSL, or the transcription factors that regulate the pathway, indicating that the accumulation of metabolic intermediates, rather than impaired DNPS, underlies the toxicity (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019; Chen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to yeast studies (Daignan-Fornier and Pinson, 2019; Chen et al., 2016).

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, ADSL loss caused delayed growth, infertility, reduced life span, and locomotion defects.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, ADSL loss caused delayed growth, infertility, reduced life span, and locomotion defects.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to C. elegans studies (Chen et al., 2016; Marsac et al., 2019; Fenton et al., 2017).

claim: In some C. elegans studies, growth, life span, and locomotion defects could be linked to the accumulation of SAICAR.
source: In some studies, growth, life span, and locomotion could be linked to the accumulation of SAICAR (Chen et al., 2016; Marsac et al., 2019; Fenton et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to C. elegans studies (Chen et al., 2016; Marsac et al., 2019; Fenton et al., 2017).

claim: Perfusion of rat brains with SAICAr caused cellular attrition in the hippocampus.
source: Perfusion of rat brains with SAICAr caused cellular attrition in the hippocampus, leading to the proposition that SAICAr accumulation is neurotoxic, although the potential mechanism remains unknown (Stone et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Stone et al., 1998.

claim: SAICAr accumulation is neurotoxic, although the potential mechanism remains unknown.
source: Perfusion of rat brains with SAICAr caused cellular attrition in the hippocampus, leading to the proposition that SAICAr accumulation is neurotoxic, although the potential mechanism remains unknown (Stone et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Stone et al., 1998.

claim: In glucose-deprived cancer cells, SAICAR accumulation was shown to activate PKM2 and other kinases to promote cancer survival.
source: In glucose-deprived cancer cells, SAICAR accumulation was shown to activate PKM2, and a number of other kinases, to promote cancer survival in glucose-limiting conditions, suggesting that purine metabolite accumulation could have distinct signaling outcomes that impact on cell behavior and fate during development (Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to cancer studies (Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016).

claim: Purine metabolite accumulation could have distinct signaling outcomes that impact on cell behavior and fate during development.
source: In glucose-deprived cancer cells, SAICAR accumulation was shown to activate PKM2, and a number of other kinases, to promote cancer survival in glucose-limiting conditions, suggesting that purine metabolite accumulation could have distinct signaling outcomes that impact on cell behavior and fate during development (Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to cancer studies (Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016).

claim: The underlying mechanisms by which neuropathology arises in ADSLD remain unknown.
source: However, despite extensive enzymology and structural information, the underlying mechanisms by which neuropathology arises in ADSLD remain unknown.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: ADSL depletion with a pool of four siRNAs in hTERT-RPE-1 cells resulted in 80% depletion of ADSL mRNA and a clear reduction in protein levels.
source: Depletion of ADSL was effective as we observed 80% depletion of the mRNA and a clear reduction in protein levels (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 1A and Western blot in Figure 1B.

claim: ADSL depletion in RPE-1 cells was accompanied by reduced levels of AMP and GMP.
source: This was accompanied by reduced levels of AMP and GMP, as well as accumulation of S-Ado (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LC-MS data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: ADSL depletion in RPE-1 cells resulted in accumulation of S-Ado.
source: This was accompanied by reduced levels of AMP and GMP, as well as accumulation of S-Ado (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LC-MS data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: SAICAr levels were at the limit of detection in RPE-1 cells and differences could not be assessed.
source: SAICAr levels were at the limit of detection in RPE-1 cells and differences could not be assessed (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LC-MS data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Elevated SAICAr could be readily observed following ADSL depletion in HeLa cells.
source: but elevated SAICAr could be readily observed following ADSL depletion in HeLa, potentially due to elevated levels of DNPS enzymes that have been observed in cancer cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Zurlo et al., 2019; Agarwal et al., 2020; Yamauchi et al., 2022; Taha-Mehlitz et al., 2021).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by LC-MS data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C with citations to cancer literature (Zurlo et al., 2019; Agarwal et al., 2020; Yamauchi et al., 2022; Taha-Mehlitz et al., 2021).

claim: ADSL depletion in RPE-1 cells reduced cell proliferation rates.
source: As ADSL is critical for DNPS, we examined cell growth following ADSL depletion and found reduced levels of proliferation in ADSL-depleted cells compared to controls (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell counting data in Figure 1D.

claim: ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells frequently lacked Ki67 expression, indicating that some cells were exiting the cell cycle.
source: ADSL-depleted cells frequently lacked Ki67 expression, indicating that some cells were exiting the cell cycle, had increased levels of p53, and showed accumulation in G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1E and flow cytometry in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells had increased levels of p53.
source: ADSL-depleted cells frequently lacked Ki67 expression, indicating that some cells were exiting the cell cycle, had increased levels of p53, and showed accumulation in G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1F.

claim: ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells showed accumulation in G1 phase of the cell cycle.
source: ADSL-depleted cells frequently lacked Ki67 expression, indicating that some cells were exiting the cell cycle, had increased levels of p53, and showed accumulation in G1 phase of the cell cycle (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by flow cytometry data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Cell death was not increased in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: Trypan Blue and β-galactosidase assays indicated that cell death was not increased (Figure 1—figure supplement 2F)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Trypan Blue assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: Ki67-negative ADSL-depleted cells were likely quiescent and not senescent.
source: and that the Ki67-negative cells were likely quiescent and not senescent (Figure 1—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by β-galactosidase assay data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2G.

claim: Deletion of TP53 rescued proliferation, prevented G1 arrest, and restored the number of Ki67-positive cells in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: Deletion of TP53 rescued proliferation, prevented G1 arrest, and restored the number of Ki67-positive cells (Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2H and I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by cell counting data in Figure 1G, flow cytometry in Figure 1—figure supplement 2H, and Ki67 staining in Figure 1—figure supplement 2I.

claim: The reduction in Ki67-positive cells in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells could be rescued by stable expression of an siRNA-resistant allele of ADSL (ADSL*).
source: The reduction in Ki67-positive cells could be rescued by stable expression of an siRNA-resistant allele of ADSL (ADSL*) (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 2J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 2J.

claim: ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells did not undergo differentiation as assessed by vimentin and cytokeratin 20 (CK20) staining.
source: We did not observe any CK20 signal or a reduction in vimentin-positive cells in the population upon ADSL silencing compared to the controls, arguing against premature differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Supplementation of ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells with nucleosides or adenosine did not prevent p53 induction or cell cycle exit.
source: Supplementation of ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells with nucleosides or adenosine did not prevent p53 induction or cell cycle exit (Figure 1I and J).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1I and J.

claim: Treatment with MRT00252040 (PAICS inhibitor) did not influence p53 induction or loss of Ki67 in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: Similarly, treatment with MRT00252040 did not influence p53 induction or loss of Ki67 (Figure 1K and L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1K and L.

claim: ADSL depletion in non-transformed human epithelial cells leads to a partial p53-dependent cell cycle exit/arrest that is not rescued by nucleoside supplementation or inhibiting PAICS.
source: This demonstrated that ADSL depletion in non-transformed human epithelial cells leads to a partial p53-dependent cell cycle exit/arrest that is not rescued by complementing the defects of ADSL depletion with nucleoside supplementation or inhibiting PAICS to prevent SAICAR/r production upstream of ADSL.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figure 1.

claim: In ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells, chromatin-bound RPA levels were increased, indicative of replication stress.
source: In ADSL-depleted cells, chromatin-bound RPA levels were increased, indicative of replication stress, although the effect was mild (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2A.

claim: ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells showed an increased number of cells with more than five 53BP1 foci per cell, indicative of DNA double-strand break (DSBs) accumulation.
source: Additionally, we observed an increased number of cells with more than five 53BP1 foci per cell, indicative of DNA double-strand break (DSBs) accumulation (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2B.

claim: 53BP1 foci in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells were reduced by treatment with a small-molecule inhibitor for ATM, indicating an active DNA damage response.
source: 53BP1 foci were reduced by treatment with a small-molecule inhibitor for ATM (Figure 2C), indicating an active DNA damage response.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2C.

claim: Supplementation of ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells with nucleosides suppressed the appearance of DNA DSBs detected by 53BP1.
source: Supplementation of cells with nucleosides suppressed the appearance of DNA DSBs detected by 53BP1 following ADSL depletion or treatment with the ribonucleotide reductase inhibitor hydroxyurea (HU) that depletes dNTP pools (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2D and E.

claim: Adenosine supplementation reduced 53BP1 foci in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: A similar reduction in 53BP1 foci was also observed with adenosine supplementation of ADSL-depleted cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2F.

claim: Nucleoside supplementation reduced the increase in γH2AX in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: Nucleoside supplementation also reduced the increase in γH2AX, the phosphorylated form of the histone variant H2AX, which is also a marker of DSBs (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2G.

claim: The PAICS inhibitor MRT00252040 did not rescue the increased levels of DSBs in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: In contrast to nucleoside supplementation, the PAICS inhibitor MRT00252040 did not rescue the increased levels of DSBs (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 2H.

claim: ADSL depletion in cultured cells induces mild levels of DNA damage signaling that can be suppressed by nucleoside supplementation, but not by the inhibition of PAICS.
source: These data indicate that ADSL depletion in cultured cells induces mild levels of DNA damage signaling that can be suppressed by nucleoside supplementation, but not by the inhibition of PAICS.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figure 2.

claim: DNA damage signaling in ADSL-depleted cells implicates defects in the purine nucleotide cycle, rather than impaired DNPS or specific metabolite accumulation.
source: This implicates defects in the purine nucleotide cycle, rather than impaired DNPS or specific metabolite accumulation resulting from ADSL depletion, in replication stress and DSB formation.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the differential rescue of DNA damage by nucleosides versus PAICS inhibition.

claim: The partial p53-dependent cell cycle exit in ADSL-depleted cells is not solely a consequence of DNA damage signaling or purine metabolite accumulation.
source: In addition, it indicates that the partial p53-dependent cell cycle exit is not solely a consequence of DNA damage signaling or purine metabolite accumulation, as it was not rescued by either intervention.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the lack of rescue of cell cycle exit by nucleosides or PAICS inhibition.

claim: Electroporation of chicken neural tubes with ADSL shRNA resulted in efficient ADSL depletion.
source: After confirming efficient ADSL depletion (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 3A.

claim: In chicken neural tubes, ADSL depletion reduced both SOX2-positive neural progenitors and ELAVL3/4-positive post-mitotic neurons.
source: We found that in the ADSL-depleted side both cell populations were reduced when compared to the non-transfected side (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3B.

claim: ADSL depletion in chicken neural tubes resulted in smaller tissue size, suggesting reduced growth and/or increased cell death.
source: and that the size of the tissue was smaller, suggesting reduced growth and/or increased cell death.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the images in Figure 3B.

claim: Staining for the apoptotic marker cleaved caspase-3 (CC3) revealed no notable differences in ADSL-depleted chicken neural tubes.
source: Staining for the apoptotic marker cleaved caspase-3 (CC3) revealed no notable differences, suggesting that this was not due to increased cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: ADSL depletion in chicken neural tubes increased the percentage of SOX2-positive progenitors relative to ELAVL3/4-positive neurons within the GFP-positive transfected cells.
source: We then analyzed SOX2 and ELAVL3/4 staining only within the GFP-positive transfected cells and found that ADSL depletion increased the percentage of SOX2-positive progenitors relative to ELAVL3/4-positive neurons (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Reduced tissue growth in ADSL-depleted chicken neural tubes was not due to premature differentiation but possibly due to a proliferation defect in the progenitor population.
source: This suggested that reduced tissue growth was not due to premature differentiation but possibly due to a proliferation defect in the progenitor population.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figure 3C.

claim: FACS analysis of GFP-positive, ELAVL3/4-negative cells in chicken neural tubes showed a slight increase in the G2/M population after ADSL depletion.
source: To study cell cycle progression in neural stem cells, we performed fluorescence-associated cell sorting (FACS) analysis of GFP-positive, ELAVL3/4-negative cells following electroporation of control or ADSL shRNA. We found that there was a slight increase in the G2/M population after ADSL depletion (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by FACS data in Figure 3D.

claim: ADSL depletion in chicken neural tubes caused a reduction in the fraction of cells that incorporated EdU.
source: Further analysis of stained tissue sections showed that ADSL depletion caused a reduction in the fraction of cells that incorporated EdU and an increase in the fraction of cells positive for the G2/M marker phosphorylated histone H3-Ser10 (pH3S10) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E.

claim: ADSL depletion in chicken neural tubes caused an increase in the fraction of cells positive for the G2/M marker phosphorylated histone H3-Ser10 (pH3S10).
source: Further analysis of stained tissue sections showed that ADSL depletion caused a reduction in the fraction of cells that incorporated EdU and an increase in the fraction of cells positive for the G2/M marker phosphorylated histone H3-Ser10 (pH3S10) (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3E.

claim: ADSL depletion in chicken neural tubes caused a specific delay in G2 phase in the SOX2+ population, rather than during mitosis.
source: We separated the pH3S10-positive cells into two populations: G2 cells, identified by punctate pH3S10 staining, and mitotic cells, displaying broadly distributed pH3S10 staining. This revealed that only the G2 fraction of cells was increased by ADSL depletion, indicating that ADSL depletion caused a specific delay in G2 phase in the SOX2+ population, rather than during mitosis (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 3F.

claim: ADSL depletion in vitro and in vivo leads to reduced cellularity in the developing brain, without a clear induction of cell death or senescence.
source: Together, our in vitro data indicate that ADSL depletion leads to a mild induction of DNA damage signaling and impaired cell cycle progression. In vivo, this manifests as reduced cellularity in the developing brain, without a clear induction of cell death or senescence.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figures 1-3.

claim: Fewer ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells had cilia after serum starvation, and the cilia that were present were shorter compared to controls.
source: Fewer cells treated with the ADSL siRNA pool had cilia, and the cilia that were present were shorter when compared to controls (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4B.

claim: Shorter cilia were also observed upon depletion with single siRNAs for ADSL in RPE-1 cells.
source: We also observed shorter cilia upon depletion with single siRNAs for ADSL (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Ciliogenesis defects in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells were not simply delayed, as similar defects were observed 72 hr after serum starvation.
source: To exclude the possibility that ciliogenesis was simply delayed, we quantified the number of ciliated cells 72 hr after serum starvation and observed a similar defect (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Defective ciliogenesis in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells was rescued by expression of an siRNA-resistant cDNA (ADSL*).
source: Defective ciliogenesis was rescued by expression of an siRNA-resistant cDNA (ADSL*), but not by nucleoside supplementation (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C.

claim: Defective ciliogenesis in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells was not rescued by nucleoside supplementation.
source: Defective ciliogenesis was rescued by expression of an siRNA-resistant cDNA (ADSL*), but not by nucleoside supplementation (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4D.

claim: Inhibition of the DNPS pathway with methotrexate (MTX) had no effect on ciliogenesis in control RPE-1 cells.
source: Inhibition of the DNPS pathway with methotrexate (MTX), which impairs steps in DNPS up- and downstream of ADSL (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), had no effect on ciliogenesis in control cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: MTX rescued both the number of ciliated cells and cilia length in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: but rescued both the number of ciliated cells and cilia length in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Treatment with the PAICS inhibitor MRT00252040 rescued ciliogenesis in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: Following ADSL depletion, we treated cells with the PAICS inhibitor MRT00252040 (Hoxhaj et al., 2017). Similar to MTX, this rescued ciliogenesis as the number and length of cilia were similar in control and ADSL-depleted cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4E with citation to Hoxhaj et al., 2017.

claim: Treatment of RPE-1 cells with SAICAr recapitulated the ciliogenesis defect observed in ADSL-depleted cells.
source: As inhibition of PAICS impairs DNPS upstream of SAICAR production, we treated cells with SAICAr and observed that this recapitulated the ciliogenesis defect observed in ADSL-depleted cells (Figure 4F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4F and G.

claim: SAICAr treatment did not activate AKT activity in RPE-1 cells.
source: SAICAr treatment did not activate AKT activity, which has recently been shown to inhibit ciliogenesis due to serum starvation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E; Walia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Western blot data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E with citation to Walia et al., 2019.

claim: Depletion of ADSL in p53 KO RPE-1 cells recapitulated the reduction in ciliated cells and cilia length compared to controls.
source: While the overall percentage of ciliated cells was slightly lower in p53 KO cells, depletion of ADSL recapitulated the result obtained in RPE-1 wt cells, a reduction in ciliated cells and cilia length compared to controls (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The kinetics of cilia removal following serum add back was similar in both control and ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: In addition, the kinetics of cilia removal following serum add back was similar in both controls and ADSL-depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Impairing DNPS specifically at the ADSL-dependent step and/or SAICAr accumulation caused by ADSL depletion impairs the generation of primary cilia.
source: We concluded that impairing DNPS specifically at the ADSL-dependent step and/or SAICAr accumulation caused by ADSL depletion impairs the generation of primary cilia.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figure 4.

claim: Centrosomes in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells had normal levels of PCNT and a normal number of centrioles.
source: Centrosomes in ADSL-depleted cells had normal levels of PCNT and a normal number of centrioles (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The removal of CP110 from the mother centriole was impaired in serum-starved, ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells.
source: However, we found that the removal of CP110 from the mother centriole, a key step in early ciliogenesis, was impaired in serum-starved, ADSL-depleted cells. Compared to controls, a larger number of ADSL-depleted cells contained centrosomes with two CP110 foci (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5B.

claim: Impaired CP110 removal in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells could be phenocopied by administration of SAICAr.
source: This could be phenocopied by administration of SAICAr and was rescued by PAICS inhibition (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5C.

claim: Impaired CP110 removal in ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells was rescued by PAICS inhibition.
source: This could be phenocopied by administration of SAICAr and was rescued by PAICS inhibition (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5D.

claim: Co-depletion of CP110 with ADSL using three different siRNAs rescued the ciliogenesis defect in RPE-1 cells.
source: Co-depletion of CP110, using three independent siRNAs, with ADSL rescued the ciliogenesis defect (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 5E.

claim: ADSL deficiency or SAICAr administration impairs primary ciliogenesis, and this can be rescued by CP110 depletion or inhibition of PAICS, but not by supplementation of purine levels.
source: These data demonstrated that ADSL deficiency or SAICAr administration impairs primary ciliogenesis, and this can be rescued by CP110 depletion or inhibition of PAICS, but not by supplementation of purine levels.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figure 5.

claim: Adsl is ubiquitously expressed at early embryonic stages in zebrafish.
source: Adsl is ubiquitously expressed at early embryonic stages and, by the 18-somite stage, highly expressed in several areas of the developing brain, including the midbrain and mesencephalon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–L.

claim: By the 18-somite stage, Adsl is highly expressed in several areas of the developing zebrafish brain, including the midbrain and mesencephalon.
source: Adsl is ubiquitously expressed at early embryonic stages and, by the 18-somite stage, highly expressed in several areas of the developing brain, including the midbrain and mesencephalon (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–L).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–L.

claim: Antibody staining demonstrated expression of Adsl in zebrafish neurons, which was abolished upon injection of either morpholino.
source: Antibody staining demonstrated expression of Adsl in neurons, which was abolished upon injection of either MO (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Examination of zebrafish embryo morphology 48 hr post fertilization (hpf) revealed pericardial edema, kinked tail, hydrocephalus, and pinhead (microcephaly) phenotypes following Adsl depletion.
source: Examination of embryo morphology 48 hr post fertilization (hpf) revealed pericardial edema, kinked tail, hydrocephalus, and pinhead (microcephaly) phenotypes (Figure 6A–E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by live imaging data in Figure 6A–E.

claim: Nearly 50% of Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos exhibited weak or absent Alcian Blue staining, indicating defects in skull formation.
source: Alcian Blue staining showed that nearly 50% of the Adsl-depleted embryos exhibited weak or absent staining (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Alcian Blue staining data in Figure 6F.

claim: Defects in skull formation in Adsl-depleted zebrafish could be largely rescued by zebrafish Adsl or human ADSL expression but not expression of a human ADSL R426H mutant.
source: Defects in skull formation could be largely rescued by zebrafish Adsl or human ADSL expression but not expression of a human ADSL R426H mutant, the most frequently observed ADSLD mutation (Figure 6F; https://www.adenylosuccinatelyasedeficiency.com/).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by Alcian Blue staining data in Figure 6F.

claim: Examination of DNA damage signaling in the developing zebrafish neural tube revealed an increase in γH2AX-positive cells following Adsl depletion.
source: Examination of DNA damage signaling in the developing neural tube revealed an increase in γH2AX-positive cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6G.

claim: Treatment with nucleosides suppressed DNA damage signaling in Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos.
source: Similar to what was observed in RPE-1 cells, treatment with nucleosides suppressed DNA damage signaling (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 6G.

claim: Adsl depletion strongly impaired normal zebrafish development, leading to DNA damage that could be suppressed with nucleoside supplementation and several phenotypes consistent with ciliary defects.
source: These data demonstrated that Adsl depletion strongly impaired normal zebrafish development, leading to DNA damage that could be suppressed with nucleoside supplementation and several phenotypes consistent with ciliary defects.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figure 6.

claim: Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos showed higher frequencies of heart looping defects, including inverse looping and no loops.
source: Adsl-depleted embryos showed higher frequencies of defects, including inverse looping and to a lesser extent no loops (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7A.

claim: A significant increase in inverse liver placement was observed in Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos compared to controls.
source: A significant increase in inverse liver placement was observed in Adsl-depleted embryos compared to controls, supporting a general defect in laterality (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7B.

claim: Asymmetric spaw mRNA localization was changed in about 40% of Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos.
source: Consistent with the altered distribution of cmcl2 and angptl3, asymmetric spaw mRNA localization was changed in about 40% of Adsl-depleted embryos.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7C.

claim: Most Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos with altered spaw localization showed symmetric patterning and a smaller fraction showed no or only weak staining.
source: Most of these embryos showed symmetric patterning and a smaller fraction of no or only weak staining.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7C.

claim: The correct asymmetric distribution of spaw mRNA in zebrafish could be largely restored by expression of mRNA encoding zebrafish Adsl.
source: The correct asymmetric distribution of spaw mRNA could be largely restored by expression of mRNA encoding zebrafish Adsl (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by in situ hybridization data in Figure 7C.

claim: KV area and cilia number were not significantly affected by Adsl depletion in zebrafish.
source: While KV area and cilia number were not significantly affected by Adsl depletion, cilia length was reduced in Adsl ATG MO-treated embryos, a phenotype that was partially rescued by co-injection of RNA encoding zebrafish Adsl (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 7D–F.

claim: Cilia length was reduced in the Kupffer's vesicle of Adsl ATG MO-treated zebrafish embryos.
source: While KV area and cilia number were not significantly affected by Adsl depletion, cilia length was reduced in Adsl ATG MO-treated embryos, a phenotype that was partially rescued by co-injection of RNA encoding zebrafish Adsl (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 7G.

claim: Reduced cilia length in Adsl-depleted zebrafish was partially rescued by co-injection of RNA encoding zebrafish Adsl.
source: While KV area and cilia number were not significantly affected by Adsl depletion, cilia length was reduced in Adsl ATG MO-treated embryos, a phenotype that was partially rescued by co-injection of RNA encoding zebrafish Adsl (Figure 7D–G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by confocal microscopy data in Figure 7G.

claim: The data from zebrafish, in combination with additional phenotypes including laterality defects and hydrocephalus, support the role of ADSL in promoting proper cilia formation or function in vivo.
source: These data, in combination with additional phenotypes, including laterality defects and hydrocephalus, support the role of ADSL in promoting proper cilia formation or function in vivo.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the data in Figure 7.

claim: Depletion of Adsl in zebrafish caused a significant reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells in the neural tube.
source: Similar to what we observed in the chicken neural tube, depletion of Adsl caused a significant reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells that could be rescued by the co-injection of RNA encoding zebrafish Adsl (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8A.

claim: The reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells in Adsl-depleted zebrafish could be rescued by co-injection of RNA encoding zebrafish Adsl.
source: Similar to what we observed in the chicken neural tube, depletion of Adsl caused a significant reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells that could be rescued by the co-injection of RNA encoding zebrafish Adsl (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8A.

claim: Treatment with MTX completely rescued the reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells in the neural tube of Adsl-depleted zebrafish.
source: Treatment with MTX completely rescued the reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells in the neural tube, indicating that this was not a result of impaired DNPS per se, but likely a consequence of intermediate metabolite accumulation (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8B.

claim: The reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells in Adsl-depleted zebrafish was not a result of impaired DNPS per se, but likely a consequence of intermediate metabolite accumulation.
source: Treatment with MTX completely rescued the reduction in Elavl3/4-positive cells in the neural tube, indicating that this was not a result of impaired DNPS per se, but likely a consequence of intermediate metabolite accumulation (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the rescue with MTX in Figure 8B.

claim: Similar results to MTX rescue of Elavl3/4-positive cells were observed with a second morpholino targeting Adsl in zebrafish.
source: Similar results were observed with a second morpholino targeting Adsl (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Depletion of Adsl reduced the number of Sox2-positive cells in the developing zebrafish forebrain.
source: Depletion of Adsl reduced the number of Sox2-positive cells, and this was rescued by co-treatment with MTX (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8C.

claim: The reduction in Sox2-positive cells in Adsl-depleted zebrafish was rescued by co-treatment with MTX.
source: Depletion of Adsl reduced the number of Sox2-positive cells, and this was rescued by co-treatment with MTX (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8C.

claim: Supplementation with nucleosides did not rescue the reduced number of Sox2-positive progenitors in Adsl-depleted zebrafish embryos.
source: In contrast, supplementation with nucleosides did not rescue the reduced number of Sox2-positive progenitors in Adsl-depleted embryos (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 8D.

claim: The data indicate a specific role of impaired DNPS, and likely SAICAr accumulation, in the neural progenitor defects associated with Adsl depletion in zebrafish.
source: These data indicate a specific role of impaired DNPS, and likely SAICAr accumulation, in the neural progenitor defects associated with Adsl depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section and supported by the differential rescue by MTX versus nucleosides in Figure 8.

claim: Multiple phenotypes associated with ADSL depletion in human RPE-1 cells, as well as developing chicken and zebrafish embryos, can largely be rescued by interventions that suppress the generation of metabolites in the DNPS pathway or restore purine levels.
source: Our results uncovered multiple phenotypes associated with ADSL depletion in human RPE-1 cells, as well as developing chicken and zebrafish embryos (Appendix 1). These can largely be rescued by interventions that suppress the generation of metabolites in the DNPS pathway or restore purine levels, complementing defective DNPS or purine nucleotide pathway activity.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data throughout the manuscript.

claim: DNA damage signaling in ADSL-depleted cells was suppressed by nucleoside supplementation in human cells and zebrafish, suggesting that this was caused by purine deficiency.
source: DNA damage signaling was suppressed by nucleoside supplementation in human cells and zebrafish, suggesting that this was caused by purine deficiency (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figures 2 and 6G.

claim: Defects in primary ciliogenesis resulting from ADSL depletion were rescued by PAICS inhibitor or MTX treatment, but not nucleosides, and phenocopied by SAICAr administration.
source: In contrast, defects in primary ciliogenesis resulting from ADSL depletion were rescued by PAICS inhibitor or MTX treatment, but not nucleosides, and phenocopied by SAICAr administration.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: The inability to rescue ciliogenesis defects with nucleoside supplementation indicated that they most likely resulted specifically from loss of ADSL, and potentially SAICAr accumulation, rather than a general deficiency in purine supply.
source: The inability to rescue these phenotypes with nucleoside supplementation indicated that they most likely resulted specifically from loss of ADSL, and potentially SAICAr accumulation, rather than a general deficiency in purine supply.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: SAICAr levels were barely detectable in RPE-1 cells, which could indicate that a very small amount of SAICAr is sufficient to provoke the phenotypes or that signaling elicited specifically from loss of the ADSL protein is responsible.
source: As SAICAr levels were barely detectable in RPE-1, it could indicate that a very small amount of SAICAr is sufficient to provoke the phenotypes or that signaling elicited specifically from loss of the ADSL protein is responsible.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the observation in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: In ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells, p53 activation and defects in cell cycle progression were insensitive to nucleoside supplementation or DNPS modulation, indicating the involvement of additional pathways.
source: In ADSL-depleted RPE-1 cells, we could also detect p53 activation and defects in cell cycle progression, in the absence of cell death or senescence, and these phenotypes were insensitive to nucleoside supplementation or DNPS modulation, indicating the involvement of additional pathways.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figure 1.

claim: Microcephaly, which is present in a subset of more severe ADSLD cases, was observed in zebrafish embryos following Adsl depletion.
source: Microcephaly, which is present in a subset of more severe ADSLD cases (Jurecka et al., 2008; Jurecka et al., 2012; Mouchegh et al., 2007), was observed in zebrafish embryos following Adsl depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to clinical literature (Jurecka et al., 2008; Jurecka et al., 2012; Mouchegh et al., 2007) and supported by the data in Figure 6.

claim: ADSL depletion in chicken embryos led to a reduction in neural tube size.
source: Similarly, ADSL depletion in chicken embryos led to a reduction in neural tube size.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figure 3.

claim: The results suggest that chicken and zebrafish are potentially valuable models for understanding the etiology of microcephaly in ADSLD.
source: Together, the results suggest that they are potentially valuable models for understanding the etiology of microcephaly in ADSLD (Jurecka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Jurecka et al., 2015 and supported by the data in Figures 3, 6, and 8.

claim: DNA damage, p53 activation, and defects in cilia function have all been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Seckel syndrome, which is associated with microcephaly.
source: DNA damage, p53 activation, and defects in cilia function, which we observed following ADSL depletion, have all been implicated in neurodevelopmental disorders, such as Seckel syndrome, which is associated with microcephaly (Stracker et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Stracker et al., 2020.

claim: In Seckel syndrome mice expressing hypomorphic, humanized alleles of Atr, replication stress and DNA damage preceded neuroprogenitor cell death.
source: In Seckel syndrome mice expressing hypomorphic, humanized alleles of Atr, replication stress and DNA damage preceded neuroprogenitor cell death (O'Driscoll et al., 2003; Murga et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to O'Driscoll et al., 2003 and Murga et al., 2009.

claim: In Seckel syndrome mice with Atr hypomorphic alleles, extensive p53 activation was observed, but co-deletion of p53 exacerbated the cellular and organismal phenotypes, indicating a protective effect of p53 induction.
source: This was accompanied by extensive p53 activation, but co-deletion of p53 exacerbated the cellular and organismal phenotypes, indicating a protective effect of p53 induction.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the cited literature.

claim: Mutations in centrosomal proteins, such as CENPJ/SAS4/CPAP or CEP63, were also implicated in Seckel syndrome.
source: Mutations in centrosomal proteins, such as CENPJ/SAS4/CPAP or CEP63, were also implicated in Seckel syndrome (Al-Dosari et al., 2010; Sir et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Al-Dosari et al., 2010 and Sir et al., 2011.

claim: In mice with CEP63 or CENPJ/SAS4 deficiency, progenitor loss resulted from mitotic delays and the activation of the USP28-53BP1-dependent mitotic surveillance pathway.
source: In contrast to mice expressing hypomorphic Atr, progenitor loss in mice with CEP63 or CENPJ/SAS4 deficiency resulted from mitotic delays and the activation of the USP28-53BP1-dependent mitotic surveillance pathway (Bazzi and Anderson, 2014; Insolera et al., 2014; Marjanović et al., 2015; McIntyre et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2020; Fong et al., 2016; Lambrus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to multiple studies (Bazzi and Anderson, 2014; Insolera et al., 2014; Marjanović et al., 2015; McIntyre et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2020; Fong et al., 2016; Lambrus et al., 2016).

claim: In mice with CEP63 or CENPJ/SAS4 deficiency, the phenotype was completely rescued by p53 co-deletion, revealing p53-dependent cell death as a main driver of the phenotype.
source: In this case, the phenotype was completely rescued by p53 co-deletion, revealing p53-dependent cell death as a main driver of the phenotype.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the cited literature.

claim: Despite some phenotypic similarities with Seckel syndrome at the cellular level, including replication stress and p53 activation, increased cell death was not detected as a result of ADSL depletion.
source: Despite some phenotypic similarities with Seckel syndrome at the cellular level, including replication stress and p53 activation, we did not detect increased cell death as a result of ADSL depletion.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2F.

claim: The reduced cellularity caused by ADSL depletion occurs in a manner mechanistically distinct from Seckel syndrome driven by ATR deficiency or centrosome duplication defects.
source: This indicated that the reduced cellularity caused by ADSL depletion occurs in a manner mechanistically distinct from Seckel syndrome driven by ATR deficiency or centrosome duplication defects.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the comparison with Seckel syndrome.

claim: GMPS (GMP synthase) was identified as a target for p53 repression following p53 activation using Nutlin-3a.
source: GMPS (GMP synthase), an essential enzyme in the purine synthesis pathway (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), was identified as a target for p53 repression following p53 activation using Nutlin-3a (Holzer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Holzer et al., 2017.

claim: GMPS was demonstrated to promote p53 stabilization in response to genotoxic stress in a manner that requires the USP7 ubiquitin protease.
source: In addition, GMPS was demonstrated to promote p53 stabilization in response to genotoxic stress in a manner that requires the USP7 ubiquitin protease (Reddy et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Reddy et al., 2014.

claim: Induction of p53 via the GMPS pathway was demonstrated to induce cell death, which was not observed clearly in any of the systems analyzed for ADSL depletion.
source: While we cannot rule out a role for this pathway in p53 stabilization following ADSL depletion, we could not rescue p53 activation with nucleoside supplementation and induction of p53 via the GMPS pathway was demonstrated to induce cell death, which we did not observe clearly in any of the systems we analyzed.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the cited literature and the data in the manuscript.

claim: Defects in cilium removal and premature progenitor differentiation have been clearly implicated in microcephaly in Seckel syndrome and primary microcephaly.
source: In addition to p53-dependent and -independent cell death, defects in cilium removal and premature progenitor differentiation have also been clearly implicated in microcephaly in Seckel syndrome and primary microcephaly (Gabriel et al., 2016; Farooq et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Gabriel et al., 2016 and Farooq et al., 2020.

claim: Analysis of cilia removal by adding back serum to serum-starved RPE-1 cells depleted for ADSL showed normal rates of cilia removal.
source: We examined the removal of cilia by adding back serum to serum-starved RPE-1 cells depleted for ADSL and observed normal rates of cilia removal (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G), suggesting that impaired cilia resorption was likely not impairing cell cycle exit and indirectly impacting ciliogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Analysis of differentiation in RPE-1 cells depleted for ADSL did not support a premature differentiation phenotype.
source: Analysis of differentiation in RPE-1 cells depleted for ADSL also did not support a premature differentiation phenotype (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2K.

claim: Cell cycle delays were observed following ADSL depletion in RPE-1 and chicken embryos.
source: In RPE-1 and chicken embryos, we observed cell cycle delays following ADSL depletion
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: An overall reduction in SOX2-positive progenitor cells was observed in both chicken and zebrafish in vivo systems following ADSL depletion.
source: as well as an overall reduction in SOX2-positive progenitor cells in both in vivo systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: Differentiated ELAVL3/4-positive cell numbers were reduced in both chicken and fish systems following ADSL depletion.
source: As a result, differentiated ELAVL3/4-positive cell numbers were also reduced in both chicken and fish systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: Cell cycle delay following ADSL depletion was further supported by the observation that, contrary to overall Sox2-positive cell numbers, the number of transfected, Sox2-positive cells in chicken embryos was increased relative to controls.
source: Cell cycle delay was further supported by the observation that, contrary to overall Sox2-positive cell numbers, the number of transfected, Sox2-positive cells in chicken embryos was increased relative to controls.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figure 3C.

claim: Nutrient restriction was shown to arrest the proliferation of neural progenitors of Xenopus larvae and zebrafish reversibly in G2, suggesting that most of the cells were quiescent.
source: In agreement with our findings, nutrient restriction was shown to arrest the proliferation of neural progenitors of Xenopus larvae and zebrafish reversibly in G2, suggesting that most of the cells were quiescent (McKeown and Cline, 2019), consistent with the lack of evidence for cell death or senescence in ADSL-depleted systems.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to McKeown and Cline, 2019.

claim: Arrest in Xenopus progenitors did not require mTOR signaling, but nutrient-dependent cell cycle reentry was mTOR dependent.
source: While arrest in Xenopus progenitors did not require mTOR signaling, nutrient-dependent cell cycle reentry was mTOR dependent.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the cited literature (McKeown and Cline, 2019).

claim: Purine deficiency inhibits the mTORC1 pathway, which regulates protein synthesis in response to nutrient availability.
source: Purine deficiency inhibits the mTORC1 pathway, which regulates protein synthesis in response to nutrient availability (Hoxhaj et al., 2017)
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Hoxhaj et al., 2017.

claim: Inactivation of mTORC1 results in microcephaly in mouse models, but this was attributed mainly to increased levels of cell death.
source: and inactivation of mTORC1 results in microcephaly in mouse models, but this was attributed mainly to increased levels of cell death (Cloëtta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Cloëtta et al., 2013.

claim: While a role for dysregulated mTOR signaling in the phenotypes associated with ADSLD cannot be ruled out, the origin of microcephaly is likely to be mechanistically distinct to that in mTORC1-deficient mouse models.
source: Thus, while we cannot rule out a role for dysregulated mTOR signaling in the phenotypes associated with ADSLD, the origin of microcephaly is likely to be mechanistically distinct to that in mTORC1-deficient mouse models.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the comparison with mTORC1-deficient models.

claim: The reduction in brain size resulting from ADSL depletion is largely due to the impaired cell cycle progression observed in SOX2-positive progenitors and delayed differentiation.
source: We therefore propose that the reduction in brain size resulting from ADSL depletion is largely due to the impaired cell cycle progression observed in SOX2-positive progenitors and delayed differentiation.
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and is based on the data in Figures 3 and 8.

claim: The molecular targets of SAICAR remain largely unclear.
source: The molecular targets of SAICAR remain largely unclear
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section.

claim: SAICAR accumulation has been linked to activation of PKM2, and other kinases, in the context of glucose deficiency in cancer.
source: but its accumulation has been linked to activation of PKM2, and other kinases, in the context of glucose deficiency in cancer (Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Keller et al., 2012; Keller et al., 2014; Yan et al., 2016.

claim: Recent work implicated ADSL in the activation of MYC, which plays a major role in controlling metabolism and proliferation in cancer cells.
source: Recent work also implicated ADSL in the activation of MYC, which plays a major role in controlling metabolism and proliferation in cancer cells (Zurlo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Zurlo et al., 2019.

claim: Modulation of central signaling pathways, including AKT and mTOR that control energetics and proliferation, may be one way by which SAICAr could affect cilia.
source: Considering that ciliogenesis is a highly regulated process and tightly coordinated with the cell cycle, modulation of central signaling pathways, including AKT and mTOR that control energetics and proliferation, may be one way by which SAICAr could affect cilia (Hoxhaj et al., 2017; Walia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citations to Hoxhaj et al., 2017 and Walia et al., 2019.

claim: AKT was shown to regulate a key step in ciliary vesicle formation and AKT activation exerts an inhibitory effect on ciliogenesis induced by serum starvation.
source: In particular, AKT was shown to regulate a key step in ciliary vesicle formation and AKT activation exerts an inhibitory effect on ciliogenesis induced by serum starvation (Walia et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Walia et al., 2019.

claim: SAICAr treatment did not result in detectable increase in AKT activation, indicating that the ability of SAICAr to inhibit ciliogenesis occurs through a distinct mechanism.
source: We examined AKT activation following SAICAr treatment and did not observe any detectable increase, indicating that the ability of SAICAr to inhibit ciliogenesis occurs through a distinct mechanism, consistent with the fact that CP110 depletion, which occurs prior to vesicle formation, rescued ciliation in ADSL-depleted cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section and supported by the data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E and Figure 5E.

claim: ADSL has been identified as a proximal interactor of numerous centrosomal proteins, including CEP104, CEP128, CEP135, CEP152, CEP89, and centrobin.
source: ADSL has also been identified as a proximal interactor of numerous centrosomal proteins, including CEP104, CEP128, CEP135, CEP152, CEP89, and centrobin, suggesting that it may play specific regulatory roles involving direct interactions or its enzymatic activity locally at centrosomes (Gupta et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the Discussion section with citation to Gupta et al., 2015.

claim: ADSL may play specific regulatory roles involving direct interactions or its enzymatic activity locally at centrosomes.
